headline: Managers' people skills drive engagement
stat_label: of the variance in team engagement comes down to the manager
fact: Gallup finds managers account for 70% of the variance in team engagement. How a manager connects with people, a core EQ skill, shapes how engaged the whole team is.
citation: Pitonyak, J., & DeSimone, R. (2022, August 9; updated 2024, January 19). How to engage frontline managers. Gallup. Also reported in Clifton, J., & Harter, J. (2019). It's the manager: Moving from boss to coach. Gallup Press.

headline: People stay for high-EQ leaders
stat_label: plan to stay 5+ years with a high-EQ leader, vs. 41% with a low-EQ leader
fact: 69% of employees led by high-EQ leaders plan to stay 5 years or more, compared with 41% of those led by low-EQ leaders.
citation: Korn Ferry. (2018). The power of EI: The "soft" skills the sharpest leaders use. Korn Ferry.

headline: Leaders with people skills keep their people
stat_label: lower turnover
fact: Leaders who consistently developed their team and built a sense of belonging, both Relationship Management skills, had 40% lower turnover than their peers.
citation: Zenger Folkman. (2024, December 6). 8 high-impact actions leaders can take to reduce turnover. Zenger Folkman.

headline: Prioritizing EQ pays off
stat_label: more likely to be high performing
fact: In a survey of more than 1,600 leaders and team members in 95 countries, organizations that made EQ development a priority were 22 times as likely to be rated high performing.
citation: Six Seconds. (2017, October 16). New research: 22x more likely to be high performing. https://www.6seconds.org/2017/10/16/new-research-eq-performance/

headline: EQ sells
stat_label: more in sales per salesperson, per year
fact: At L'Oréal, salespeople hired for their emotional competencies sold $91,370 more per year than salespeople hired the usual way, for a net revenue gain of more than $2.5 million.
citation: Cherniss, C. (1999). The business case for emotional intelligence. Consortium for Research on Emotional Intelligence in Organizations. (Reporting Spencer & Spencer, 1993, and Spencer, McClelland, & Kelner, 1997.)

headline: EQ can be trained
stat_label: studies show training raises EQ
fact: Emotional intelligence can be trained. Across 58 studies, EQ training had a moderate, positive effect.
citation: Mattingly, V., & Kraiger, K. (2019). Can emotional intelligence be trained? A meta-analytical investigation. Human Resource Management Review, 29(2), 140–155.

headline: Most of us overrate our self-awareness
stat_label: of people studied were truly self-aware
fact: Most people believe they're self-aware, but only 10% to 15% of people studied actually met the criteria.
citation: Eurich, T. (2018, January 4). What self-awareness really is (and how to cultivate it). Harvard Business Review.

headline: Your mood reaches further than you think
stat_label: more likely to be happy when a nearby friend is
fact: Emotions are contagious. When a friend who lives within a mile becomes happy, you're about 25% more likely to be happy too. Managing your own mood has a ripple effect.
citation: Fowler, J. H., & Christakis, N. A. (2008). Dynamic spread of happiness in a large social network: Longitudinal analysis over 20 years in the Framingham Heart Study. BMJ, 337, a2338.

headline: Leaders' EQ drives better leadership
stat_label: studies link leader EQ to performance
fact: Leaders' EQ goes with better leadership. A review of 101 studies linked it to stronger leadership behaviors and better performance outcomes.
citation: Gerhardt, K., Bauwens, R., & van Woerkom, M. (2026). Emotional intelligence and leader outcomes: A comprehensive review and roadmap for future inquiry. Human Resource Development Review, 25(1), 29–79.

headline: Women have an edge in reading others
fact: Across 609,278 people in 76 countries, women scored higher in emotional intelligence on average, with the biggest edge in reading other people's emotions. On self-assessments, the gap was small.
citation: Hausfeld, M. M., Hampel, V., Bach, L. J., & Menges, J. I. (2026). Putting assumptions to the test: A meta-analytic review of gender differences in emotional intelligence and specific emotion abilities. Emotion.

headline: Gratitude is contagious
fact: When leaders say thank you, employees start noticing what coworkers do for them, thank each other more, and build stronger working relationships. A simple Relationship Management habit spreads.
citation: Locklear, L. R., Kane, M. E., & Ehrhart, M. G. (2026). Grateful leaders and attentive followers: How grateful attention transmits the cascade of gratitude expressions to strengthen coworker relationships. Journal of Applied Psychology.

headline: Experience builds emotional clarity
fact: Older graduate students reported more emotional clarity and a better ability to repair a bad mood, two EQ skills that grow with experience.
citation: Aragundi-Moncada, J. G., Bueno-Fernández, M. M., Espinoza-Solís, E., Guillén-Rodríguez, A. P., Sabando García, Á. R., Lamus de Rodríguez, T. M., Ultreras-Rodríguez, A., & Moreira-Choez, J. S. (2025). The relationship between age and emotional intelligence in postgraduate students. Frontiers in Education, 10, 1558339.

headline: Calm spreads too
fact: Teaching some people in a group to reframe upsetting events, a Self-Management skill, also lowered negative feelings in the people who weren't trained.
citation: Pinus, M., Cao, Y., Halperin, E., Coman, A., Gross, J. J., & Goldenberg, A. (2025). Emotion regulation contagion drives reduction in negative intergroup emotions. Nature Communications, 16, 1387.

headline: Well-being protects caregivers from burnout
stat_label: points less burnout for every 1-point rise in well-being
fact: In a study of 260 hospital staff, higher emotional well-being went with less burnout: every 1-point rise meant 2.5 points less burnout. Staff who took on other people's emotions most strongly burned out more. Caring for others starts with caring for yourself.
citation: El Naggar, M. A., AL-Mutairi, S. M., Al Saidan, A. A., Al-Rashedi, O. S., AL-Mutairi, T. A., Al-Ruwaili, O. S., AL-Mutairi, B. Z., AL-Mutairi, N. M., AL-Mutairi, F. S., & Alrashedi, A. S. (2025). Emotional intelligence and burnout in healthcare professionals: A hospital-based study. Healthcare, 13(15), 1840.

headline: Stress is catching
fact: On teams where moods spread easily, people's well-being took a bigger hit under stress. Managing your own stress protects your team too.
citation: Hernandez Grande, A., Farr-Wharton, B., Sharafizad, F., Darcy, S., & Gavin, M. (2025). Catching on: Work stress, employee wellbeing, and the moderating role of team-level emotional contagion. Journal of Management & Organization, 31(1), 346–359.

headline: Smiles travel over video
fact: On video calls, smiles spread within seconds. Anger and sadness spread too but barely show on camera, so Social Awareness online means checking in with words.
citation: Marx, A. K. G., Sachs, D. F., Frenzel, A. C., & Schweizer, M. T. (2025). Emotional contagion in dyadic online video conferences: Empirical evidence based on self-report and facial expression data. Frontiers in Psychology, 16, 1546303.

headline: Engaged teams sell more
stat_label: higher sales productivity in the most engaged business units
fact: Business units in the top quarter of employee engagement are 18% more productive in sales than those in the bottom quarter. Engagement grows when leaders connect with their people, a core EQ skill.
citation: Gallup. (2024). The relationship between engagement at work and organizational outcomes: 2024 Q12 meta-analysis (11th ed.). Gallup, Inc.

headline: Workplace EQ gains last
stat_label: months after training, gains still held
fact: EQ training at work pays off beyond the workshop. Across 50 studies, gains lasted more than three months.
citation: Mehler, M., Balint, E., Gralla, M., Pößnecker, T., Gast, M., Hölzer, M., Kösters, M., & Gündel, H. (2024). Training emotional competencies at the workplace: A systematic review and metaanalysis. BMC Psychology, 12, 718.

headline: IQ only goes so far
stat_label: of the differences in job performance come down to IQ
fact: Decades of research put IQ at about 10% to 25% of the differences in how well people do their jobs. That leaves most of performance to other skills, including emotional intelligence.
citation: Schmidt, F. L., & Hunter, J. E. (1998). The validity and utility of selection methods in personnel psychology: Practical and theoretical implications of 85 years of research findings. Psychological Bulletin, 124(2), 262–274. Sackett, P. R., Zhang, C., Berry, C. M., & Lievens, F. (2022). Revisiting meta-analytic estimates of validity in personnel selection: Addressing systematic overcorrection for restriction of range. Journal of Applied Psychology, 107(11), 2040–2068.

headline: Companies want EQ at the top
stat_label: years of rising demand for social skills in executive hiring
fact: Companies want EQ at the top. Over 17 years, executive job descriptions asked more and more for social skills like listening and empathy, especially at larger, more complex organizations.
citation: Hansen, S., Ramdas, T., Sadun, R., & Fuller, J. (2021). The demand for executive skills (NBER Working Paper No. 28959). National Bureau of Economic Research.

headline: Leaders set the emotional tone
stat_label: studies show leaders' moods spread to their teams
fact: Across 25 studies, leaders' good moods spread to their teams, especially when the leaders were energizing and inspiring. Self-aware leaders can set the tone on purpose.
citation: Clarkson, B. G., Wagstaff, C. R. D., Arthur, C. A., & Thelwell, R. C. (2020). Leadership and the contagion of affective phenomena: A systematic review and mini meta-analysis. European Journal of Social Psychology, 50(1), 61–80.

headline: A face doesn't tell the whole story
fact: A facial expression alone isn't a reliable read on how someone feels. The same scowl can mean anger, concentration, or a headache. Social Awareness means taking in the whole situation, and asking.
citation: Barrett, L. F., Adolphs, R., Marsella, S., Martinez, A. M., & Pollak, S. D. (2019). Emotional expressions reconsidered: Challenges to inferring emotion from human facial movements. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 20(1), 1–68.

headline: Neutral is a real feeling
fact: Feeling neutral is a real feeling, and a common one. People report it about as often as positive feelings. Self-Awareness includes noticing the quiet emotions too.
citation: Gasper, K., Spencer, L. A., & Hu, D. (2019). Does neutral affect exist? How challenging three beliefs about neutral affect can advance affective research. Frontiers in Psychology, 10, 2476.

headline: EQ training works under pressure
stat_label: months later, police officers' gains still held
fact: A four-session EQ program for police officers improved their emotional intelligence, empathy, resilience, and stress management compared with officers who didn't take it, and the gains still held three months later.
citation: Romosiou, V., Brouzos, A., & Vassilopoulos, S. P. (2019). An integrative group intervention for the enhancement of emotional intelligence, empathy, resilience and stress management among police officers. Police Practice and Research, 20(5), 460–478.

headline: High-EQ leaders lift their teams
fact: When leaders have higher EQ, their employees perform better and go the extra mile, in every culture studied.
citation: Miao, C., Humphrey, R. H., & Qian, S. (2018). A cross-cultural meta-analysis of how leader emotional intelligence influences subordinate task performance and organizational citizenship behavior. Journal of World Business, 53(4), 463–474.

headline: EQ training sticks
stat_label: studies show gains hold up over time
fact: EQ training sticks. Across 24 studies, people kept their gains when they were checked again later.
citation: Hodzic, S., Scharfen, J., Ripoll, P., Holling, H., & Zenasni, F. (2018). How efficient are emotional intelligence trainings: A meta-analysis. Emotion Review, 10(2), 138–148.

headline: Values and connection drive happiness at work
stat_label: lawyers and judges studied
fact: In a study of more than 6,200 lawyers and judges, happiness had little to do with grades, income, or prestige. It tracked with feeling connected to others, having a say in their work, and doing work that matched their values, which EQ helps people see and build.
citation: Krieger, L. S., & Sheldon, K. M. (2015). What makes lawyers happy? A data-driven prescription to redefine professional success. George Washington Law Review, 83(2), 554–627.

headline: People leave managers
stat_label: of U.S. adults have left a job to get away from their manager
fact: In a Gallup study of 7,272 U.S. adults, one in two had left a job at some point in their career to get away from their manager. How managers handle people, an EQ skill, decides who stays.
citation: Gallup. (2015). State of the American manager: Analytics and advice for leaders. Gallup, Inc.

headline: Read the whole person
fact: From faces alone, people couldn't tell whether tennis players had just won or lost a point. With the body in view, it was easy. Social Awareness means reading body language and context along with faces.
citation: Aviezer, H., Trope, Y., & Todorov, A. (2012). Body cues, not facial expressions, discriminate between intense positive and negative emotions. Science, 338(6111), 1225–1229.

headline: EQ adds what IQ and personality miss
fact: A meta-analysis of emotional intelligence studies found EQ predicts job performance even after accounting for personality and IQ.
citation: O'Boyle, E. H., Jr., Humphrey, R. H., Pollack, J. M., Hawver, T. H., & Story, P. A. (2011). The relation between emotional intelligence and job performance: A meta-analysis. Journal of Organizational Behavior, 32(5), 788–818.

headline: Higher EQ, better health
fact: Two meta-analyses found people with higher emotional intelligence tend to have better mental and physical health.
source: Martins et al., 2010; Schutte et al., 2007
citation: Martins, A., Ramalho, N., & Morin, E. (2010). A comprehensive meta-analysis of the relationship between emotional intelligence and health. Personality and Individual Differences, 49(6), 554–564. Schutte, N. S., Malouff, J. M., Thorsteinsson, E. B., Bhullar, N., & Rooke, S. E. (2007). A meta-analytic investigation of the relationship between emotional intelligence and health. Personality and Individual Differences, 42(6), 921–933.

headline: Culture shapes how we read emotions
fact: East Asian viewers focused on the eyes to read emotion, while Western viewers looked across the whole face. Reading emotions across cultures takes Social Awareness.
citation: Jack, R. E., Blais, C., Scheepers, C., Schyns, P. G., & Caldara, R. (2009). Cultural confusions show that facial expressions are not universal. Current Biology, 19(18), 1543–1548.

headline: Reading emotions changes with age
fact: Older adults had more trouble recognizing some emotions, especially anger and sadness. Social Awareness habits, like asking how someone feels, help at every age.
citation: Ruffman, T., Henry, J. D., Livingstone, V., & Phillips, L. H. (2008). A meta-analytic review of emotion recognition and aging: Implications for neuropsychological models of aging. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 32(4), 863–881.

headline: Context changes what we see
fact: Japanese participants took the faces around a person into account when judging their emotion more than Western participants did. Social Awareness includes reading the room.
citation: Masuda, T., Ellsworth, P. C., Mesquita, B., Leu, J., Tanida, S., & Van de Veerdonk, E. (2008). Placing the face in context: Cultural differences in the perception of facial emotion. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 94(3), 365–381.

headline: EQ skills last for years
stat_label: years later, the skills were still there
fact: EQ skills built in a graduate business program were still there up to seven years later.
citation: Boyatzis, R. E., & Saatcioglu, A. (2008). A 20-year view of trying to develop emotional, social and cognitive intelligence competencies in graduate management education. Journal of Management Development, 27(1), 92–108.

headline: Name it to tame it
fact: Putting a feeling into words calms the brain's alarm system, the amygdala. Naming emotions is a core Self-Awareness and Self-Management tool.
citation: Lieberman, M. D., Eisenberger, N. I., Crockett, M. J., Tom, S. M., Pfeifer, J. H., & Way, B. M. (2007). Putting feelings into words: Affect labeling disrupts amygdala activity in response to affective stimuli. Psychological Science, 18(5), 421–428.

headline: EQ can make up for IQ
fact: EQ can make up for IQ. Among full-time employees, EQ was more strongly linked to supervisor-rated job performance for people with lower cognitive ability.
citation: Côté, S., & Miners, C. T. H. (2006). Emotional intelligence, cognitive intelligence, and job performance. Administrative Science Quarterly, 51(1), 1–28.

headline: Higher EQ, more effective leaders
stat_label: senior executives studied
fact: In a study of 41 senior executives, those with higher EQ, measured by an ability test, were rated more effective leaders, and EQ explained differences that personality and IQ did not.
citation: Rosete, D., & Ciarrochi, J. (2005). Emotional intelligence and its relationship to workplace performance outcomes of leadership effectiveness. Leadership & Organization Development Journal, 26(5), 388–399.

headline: Pressure can wear down well-being
fact: In law school, students' well-being and inner motivation dropped during the first year, and the declines lasted. Self-Management skills help people protect their well-being under pressure.
citation: Sheldon, K. M., & Krieger, L. S. (2004). Does legal education have undermining effects on law students? Evaluating changes in motivation, values, and well-being. Behavioral Sciences & the Law, 22(2), 261–286.

headline: One good mood lifts the whole team
fact: Groups with one cheerful member cooperated more, had less conflict, and rated their own performance higher. Managing your mood is an EQ skill that lifts the whole team.
citation: Barsade, S. G. (2002). The ripple effect: Emotional contagion and its influence on group behavior. Administrative Science Quarterly, 47(4), 644–675.

headline: Top performers win on emotional skills
stat_label: abilities that set top performers apart are emotional competencies
fact: In an analysis of competency models from 121 organizations, two out of three abilities that set top performers apart were emotional competencies.
citation: Goleman, D. (1998). Working with emotional intelligence. Bantam Books.

headline: Manager coaching makes training stick
stat_label: better results when managers coach after training
fact: Across nine studies, adding manager coaching to training raised performance results by 23% on average. Coaching is a Relationship Management skill that helps EQ training stick.
citation: Wilson Learning Worldwide. (n.d.). The impact of manager coaching on learning transfer [Research report].
